Thanks for raising this, it's worth thinking about architecturally early.  Looking at the current code, there's already an interesting foundation: HealthDataSource distinguishes .bridge (WHOOP BLE → Rust), .local (HealthKit), and .live (direct sensor) sources, and the Rust bridge operates on abstract metric methods (metrics.heart_rate_features, metrics.hrv_features) rather than WHOOP-specific calls. The HealthKit sleep importer already shows a second data path alongside BLE.  The natural seam for a device abstraction would be WhoopDataSignalPipeline, that's where WHOOP-specific packet ingestion lives. A WearableDataProvider protocol sitting above it could let Goose route data from other BLE devices through the same Rust analytics pipeline without touching the UI or algorithm layers. A few questions that would shape the design:
    - Is the Rust core's packet schema WHOOP-specific, or is it already normalized enough to accept data from other sensors?
      - Are there plans to keep Goose WHOOP-first for now, with other devices as optional backends later?
I'd be interested in helping think through the provider abstraction if that's a direction worth exploring.

## Update — HRV, respiratory rate, and resting HR now decode from WHOOP 4.0 captures (verified locally; on-device display pending a fresh sync)

**TL;DR:** The WHOOP 4.0 strap computes the recovery sensors itself and ships them inside every V24 `normal_history` history frame — the app just wasn't reading them. Three of the four now decode and pass the readiness gate as user-visible recovery metrics. This is **verified locally** by replaying a real owned capture through the bridge; confirming the rendered values **on the device** after a fresh history sync is the remaining step. SpO2 and skin-temperature stay blocked for a fundamental reason (no reference to calibrate against), not a missing decoder.

Work is on our fork, branch [`feat/whoop-4.0-gen4-support`](https://github.com/po-sc/goose/tree/feat/whoop-4.0-gen4-support) — pipeline commit [`f7cc2fd`](https://github.com/po-sc/goose/commit/f7cc2fd), parser commit [`ea6874f`](https://github.com/po-sc/goose/commit/ea6874f), shipped in PR #19.

### What we found
A sync delivered 1377 `HISTORICAL_DATA` (type-47) frames. Decoding the V24 `normal_history` body showed the strap embeds its own DSP output in each frame: RR intervals (ms), SpO2 red/ir, skin-temp raw, respiratory raw. Field offsets follow the openwhoop layout and were confirmed by the heart-rate marker matching.

### What now decodes (verified locally against a real owned capture)
| Metric | Value on the test capture | How it's validated |
|---|---|---|
| **HRV (RMSSD)** | **~42 ms** | Real consecutive beats (e.g. `[693,690]`, `[661,653]`); RMSSD in the normal 20–100 ms range. No calibration needed (RR ms → RMSSD ms). |
| **Respiratory rate** | **~15.4 rpm** | Physiological (normal 12–20); device-native `÷200` scale; matches WHOOP reporting one value per sleep. |
| **Resting HR** | **~78 bpm** | HR marker + low-motion filter (daytime capture; lower during sleep). |

"Verified locally" = the whole chain (decode → bridge → the exact `user_visible_value_allowed` field the UI reads) was exercised through `handle_bridge_request_json` against the exported capture DB. `hrv_rmssd_ms` and `respiratory_rate_rpm` come back `user_visible_value_allowed=true` with the values above. Full metric + protocol test suites stay green.

Key implementation points:
- **Re-parse the raw `payload_hex`** in the metric pipeline instead of the stored `parsed_payload_json`. The stored JSON was decoded on-device by an older parser that predates the DSP decode, so it lacked RR. Re-parsing the raw bytes is parser-version independent and means already-captured data decodes without a re-sync.
- **Segment-aware RMSSD.** A naive RMSSD over the flat concatenated RR series crosses capture-window boundaries (beats from different windows aren't adjacent) and inflated RMSSD to ~452 ms. Differencing only *within* a frame's consecutive RR, plus a Malik 20% artifact filter, gives the physiological ~42 ms. The versioned `goose_hrv_v0` is left untouched; only the report's exposed value is corrected.
- **Trust gate.** `normal_history` is added to the trusted summary-kind allowlist. An owned CoreBluetooth capture (`source=ios.corebluetooth.notification`, `sensitivity=user-owned-capture`) makes the strap's own RR a promotable, user-visible metric.
- **Respiratory `packet_k=24`.** All V24 frames are k24, but the plan only handled k18 → 0 candidates. Added a k24 arm (`body[63]`, `u16 rpm ×200`).

### Still blocked, and why (a conclusion, not a TODO)
- **SpO2** — pulse oximetry needs an AC/DC ratio-of-ratios and a factory calibration curve. From the bare red/ir values (R≈0.934) you cannot honestly derive an absolute %. Candidates decode but are not promoted.
- **Skin temperature** — the raw→°C scale gives a plausible median (~37.7 °C) but an implausible spread (24–45 °C), so the scale cannot be trusted without a WHOOP reference value. Kept gated as `temperature_units_unverified`.

This is a deliberate honesty constraint: the test device had **no WHOOP subscription/app**, so there were no reference values to calibrate against. Only metrics that need no calibration (HRV) or whose device-native scale is unambiguously physiological (respiratory) were promoted.

### Open / next
- **Confirm on-device rendering** after a fresh history sync. On a freshly reinstalled build the app currently shows only the live heart rate until a sync repopulates the local history DB; the daily Recovery widget is also scoped to the current day, so it needs same-day data. The detailed Health rows read all-time data and should show the values above once history is present.
- **Recovery score** is wired (`goose_recovery_v0`) and will compute once a few days of history accumulate — it is baseline-relative (today's HRV vs your personal norm), so it needs multi-day data by design.

### Added: metric decoder pipeline (commit f7cc2fd)

Extends this PR by wiring the decoded V12/V24 `normal_history` DSP sensors into the recovery metric pipeline so they become user-visible metrics:

- **HRV (RMSSD ~42 ms)**, **respiratory rate (~15.4 rpm)**, **resting HR (~78 bpm)** now decode and pass the readiness gate — **verified locally** by replaying a real owned capture through `handle_bridge_request_json` (the exact JSON path the UI reads). On-device rendering after a fresh sync is the remaining confirmation step.
- **SpO2** and **skin-temperature** stay intentionally gated — they need a factory/reference calibration this device (no WHOOP app) can't provide.

Full rationale, validation, and the "what's blocked and why" breakdown are in #21. Test suites stay green.

### Update — type-47 history now arrives after the Gen4 sync changes in PR #19

The dropped-reassembly behaviour was observed while the strap was in high-frequency / raw-motion mode. PR #19 stops sending `enter_high_freq_sync` before `history_start`, so the band returns ordinary `normal_history` frames instead — and a fresh sync then delivered **1377 `HISTORICAL_DATA` (type-47) frames** that reassemble cleanly.

So this appears addressed by the sync changes rather than by a reassembly-layer fix. Those frames are exactly where the recovery sensors live, and decoding them is what unblocked the metrics in #21. Leaving this open until it's confirmed across more captures/devices.

## Update 2 — verified against a real on-device capture; +Strain; perf fix

Pulled the app's own database off the device (`xcrun devicectl device copy from --domain-type appDataContainer`, 147 MB, 4852 type-47 frames) and ran the **exact bridge methods the Swift app calls** against it:

- **HRV 61.9 ms, Resting HR 80 bpm, Respiratory 15.4 rpm** — all `user_visible_value_allowed=true` on the real capture.
- **Strain `score_0_to_21 = 12.3`, pass=true** — a fourth working metric. It's computed from HR zones and does **not** need a multi-day baseline, so it works from a single session. The app already has the row + bridge call wired (`metrics.strain_score_from_features`).

Notes for anyone reproducing on-device:
- The packet-input batch (HRV/Resp/Resting HR/Vitals) runs automatically on the Health Monitor screen but iterates ~16k frames across ~20 methods, so first results take ~15–25 s — wait for "Bridge packet-derived inputs extracted" before concluding it's empty.
- The score batch (**Strain**/Recovery/Sleep/Stress) is behind the **"Run Packet-Derived Scores"** button — it does not auto-run.
- Perf: `hrv_feature_from_normal_history` was re-parsing the raw payload of *every* frame (including the high-volume raw-motion stream) just to filter; now gated on `packet_type == HISTORICAL_DATA` ([`a9352c5`](https://github.com/po-sc/goose/commit/a9352c5)).

Still blocked for the documented reasons: **Recovery** needs a personal baseline (3–4 days) + overnight sleep/strain (the test capture was a 3.4 h evening, no sleep); **SpO2** needs factory ratio-of-ratios calibration; **skin-temperature** scale can't be validated without a WHOOP reference (its candidate field is also the most variable in the frame, the opposite of a temperature signal).

@tigercraft4 thank you for the genuinely excellent file-by-file review — it caught a real latent bug and the framing on each point was spot on. Went through all four:

**Issue 1 — `supportsV5*` naming** ✅ Renamed to `supportsHistoricalSync` / `supportsAlarmCommands` / `supportsClockCommands` / `supportsSensorCommands` across all four files (`c6df20c`). You're right that a future contributor branching on the V5 name would have built the wrong frame.

**Issue 2 — hardcoded BLE delays** ✅ Extracted as `gen4HistoryKickoffDelay` (0.7 s) and `gen4HistoryPreambleStepDelay` (0.2 s) named constants (`c6df20c`), with a note that the event-driven kickoff off the `get_name` response is the better long-term fix. Agreed that's the robust version once there's hardware to test the connection-interval edge cases against.

**Issue 3 — respiratory promoted on single-device self-validation** — kept it user-visible because the device owner has no WHOOP app to cross-check against and explicitly wanted the value shown, but your concern is valid, so it carries the honest `respiratory_units_device_native_scale_accepted_no_reference` quality flag rather than claiming verification. Your `resolved_provisional` suggestion is the right model — distinguishing "reference-verified" from "self-validated on one device" — and I've noted it as the proper follow-up. Worth noting: your own PR #16 treats the same field as self-validated, which I take as independent confirmation that the V24 scale genuinely can't be reference-validated without a second device or the official app.

**Issue 4 — RMSSD post-patch over `goose_hrv_v0`** ✅ Added unit tests for `rmssd_segment_aware` (`303f329`) covering the 300/2000 ms physiological band, the Malik 20% adjacent-difference rule, and the never-difference-across-windows property — so the value that actually reaches the UI is now under test (your option 3). I kept the post-patch deliberately so `goose_hrv_v0` stays byte-stable for its versioned tests, but I agree a `goose_hrv_v1` that takes `segments: &[Vec<f64>]` directly is the cleaner end state and is the natural next step.

---

**New work since the review** (all verified against a real on-device capture pulled with `devicectl copy`):

- **Verified the full pipeline on real device data**: HRV 61.9 ms, Resting HR 80 bpm, Respiratory 15.4 rpm all come back `user_visible_value_allowed=true`.
- **Strain is a fourth working metric** (`score_0_to_21 ≈ 12.3`) — it needs no multi-day baseline, so it works from a single session; it was just behind the manual score button.
- **`body_hex` storage fix** (`3eef377`): the cached parsed-payload JSON duplicated `payload_hex` in a `body_hex` field — ~43 MB of a 147 MB DB on the raw-motion stream, scaling linearly with wear time. Dropped for large frames; HRV/resting HR/strain are byte-identical, the metric batch is ~27% faster, and multi-day captures stay bounded.
- **Scores now run off-main and auto-start** (`315a2ea`): the sleep/strain/recovery/stress batch no longer freezes the UI behind a button.

Thanks again — the review materially improved this.

Excellent root-cause analysis — confirmed and reproduced. The same bug exists in the fork and the proposed fix is correct.

`shouldDispatchNotificationSideEffectsToMain` was excluding `historicalData (47)` and `historicalIMUDataStream (52)` from main-thread dispatch as a deliberate performance optimisation for live-stream frames. The side effect is that during a historical sync, those packets are routed to the raw spool but never reach `handleHistoricalSyncValue`, so `historicalPacketsReceivedThisSync` stays at zero and the sync fails on the idle timer after three attempts — even though the band is streaming correctly.

Applied in our fork at commit `5b966fe` with the fix you proposed (guard on `isHistoricalSyncing`): historical body packets are dispatched to the main handler only while a sync is active, leaving the performance optimisation intact for live capture.

This also explains the failures reported in #22 on WHOOP 5.0 — same root cause, not a pairing issue.

For the WHOOP 5.0 cases (Umpaaa, PascalTrm) — re-pairing does not fix this because the root cause is in the app, not the BLE connection.

The issue was just identified and documented in detail in #24 by NicolasBataille: `shouldDispatchNotificationSideEffectsToMain` in `GooseBLEClient+PeripheralDelegate.swift` excludes `historicalData (packet type 47)` and `historicalIMUDataStream (52)` from main-thread dispatch as a performance optimisation for live capture. During a historical sync this means the body packets never reach the sync handler, `historicalPacketsReceivedThisSync` stays at zero, and the sync fails on the idle timer — even though the band is actually streaming correctly.

Fix applied in our fork (`5b966fe`): route these packet types to the main handler when `isHistoricalSyncing` is true, leaving them off-main otherwise. Should land upstream shortly via #24.

The WHOOP 4.0 RTC clock sync is working in [tigercraft4/goose](https://github.com/tigercraft4/goose) (commits `7b6307c`, `8c001d6`).

The `GET_CLOCK` timeout you were hitting was a generation detection issue — the command was being sent over the Gen5 command characteristic (`FD4B0002`) before the Gen4 one (`61080002`) was identified, so the band never responded. Once generation detection runs at connection time and the correct characteristic is used, `GET_CLOCK` completes normally.

What the current implementation does after connecting a WHOOP 4.0:
1. Sends `GET_CLOCK` over `61080002`
2. Reads the strap timestamp from the response body
3. Compares to iPhone time
4. If drift exceeds the threshold (5 s default), automatically sends `SET_CLOCK` with the current Unix timestamp

No user action required — the sync is silent on every connect.

The architecture question raised here was exactly the decision we faced in the fork. The approach we landed on: keep `Rust/core/` as a single shared crate and gate platform-specific code with `cfg` flags.

Concretely — iOS-only dependencies (`tungstenite` for the debug WebSocket server) are gated out when building for Android targets, and Android JNI entry points are added in a thin `bridge_android.rs` shim that calls the same `handle_bridge_request_json` function the iOS bridge uses. The Rust core — protocol parsing, SQLite persistence, metric algorithms, FFI contract — is unchanged and shared across both platforms.

The decision is documented in `docs/ADR-android-jni.md` in [tigercraft4/goose](https://github.com/tigercraft4/goose) if it's useful as a reference for the main repo.

The fork ([tigercraft4/goose](https://github.com/tigercraft4/goose)) has laid Android JNI foundations if you want to build on top rather than start from scratch.

The approach: the existing `Rust/core/` crate is shared unchanged — no duplication. Android-specific code lives in a thin JNI shim (`bridge_android.rs`) that exposes `Java_com_goose_core_GooseBridge_handleJson` and calls the same `handle_bridge_request_json` function the iOS side uses. Platform gating is done with `cfg(target_os = "android")` / `cfg(not(...))` so the iOS static library build is unaffected.

The foundation covers the FFI contract and Cargo target setup (`aarch64-linux-android`, `armv7-linux-androideabi`, `x86_64-linux-android`). The Android UI layer (Kotlin/Compose, BLE stack, JNI glue on the Kotlin side) is not yet implemented — that's where a Kotlin contributor would plug in. Happy to coordinate if you want to build on this rather than parallel-track it.

Thanks @tigercraft4 — this is really helpful. The `cfg`-flag approach with a thin `bridge_android.rs` shim is exactly the kind of concrete validation this discussion needed. The fact that it calls the same `handle_bridge_request_json` as the iOS bridge is the key point — it confirms the shared core stays clean without platform-specific conditionals leaking in.

I'll link `docs/ADR-android-jni.md` from your fork here for anyone picking this up later: https://github.com/tigercraft4/goose

@jakobrmarrone this is the missing piece — thank you. Reverse-engineering the cmd 34 → 22 → 23 sequence (and especially that Gen4 needs the single `0x00` arg byte and that cmd 22's `0x02` is a success ack, not Gen5 PENDING) from a PacketLogger capture of the official app is exactly the rigor this needed.

For context: my PR #19 implemented Gen4 framing + the V12/V24 `normal_history` DSP decode (HRV RR intervals, respiratory, skin temp) and the recovery-metric pipeline, but my historical-sync path **skipped cmd 34 and sent cmd 22 with an empty body** — which, per your findings, the strap silently drops. That's why a multi-day backlog never came off the band in my testing; the decode was ready but nothing fed it.

I've put your sync branch and my decode together on an integration branch (jakob's cmd 34→22→23 + the V24 metric decode + segment-aware RMSSD + a body_hex storage-compaction fix), and it builds cleanly — so a synced backlog now also surfaces HRV / respiratory / resting HR / strain. One small note for anyone combining the two: the Rust `parse_device_type` / `expected_device_type` only accepted `"GEN_4"`, but the Gen4 client sends `"GEN4"`, so that string needs adding in `bridge.rs` + `capture_correlation/import/fixtures.rs`.

Happy to coordinate so the sync + decode land together rather than conflicting.

Tested your sync on a real WHOOP 4.0 (multi-day backlog) merged with the #19 metric decode — **it works end to end**:

- `cmd 34 → 22 → 23` runs exactly as documented; `GET_DATA_RANGE` returns `last_synced` and the strap streams pages (`HISTORICAL_DATA` 0 → 382 → growing on a fresh install). Confirmed your note that the Swift `packets=0` per page is fine — the Rust pipeline reassembles them.
- Feeding the synced frames through the V12/V24 decode gives real metrics: **HRV pass=true, 134 RR, RMSSD 52.8 ms; respiratory candidates from every frame.** So a synced backlog now surfaces HRV / respiratory / resting HR / strain.

**One open problem — sync speed**, and I think you'll know the answer fastest. On this band the backlog is ~27k pages (`page_current≈61458`, `last_synced≈34274`), and it syncs at **~15 pages/min → ~30 h** for the full catch-up. Timing per page: `cmd 23 → HistoryStart → (≈3 s) → HistoryEnd → next cmd 23`. Each page is ~9 small frames (~860 B), i.e. ~290 B/s — far below BLE throughput, so it looks latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound.

The cmd 23 args carry `page_count = 16`, but `handleHistoryEnd` advances `gen4HistoricalPageSeq += 1` and immediately queues the next cmd 23 — so effectively one page per round-trip. **Question:** in your PacketLogger capture of the official app, does a single cmd 23 with `page_count=16` actually stream ~16 pages back-to-back (and the app advances by 16), or does the strap genuinely send one page per request? If it can burst, *not* re-issuing cmd 23 on every HistoryEnd (advancing by the count received instead) could be ~16× faster. Also: does the official app sync newest-first so recent recovery shows quickly, or strictly oldest-first like here?

Happy to test any variant on the hardware. The combined branch is `po-sc/goose@integrate/gen4-sync-plus-metrics` if useful.

Hi @Czen0596 ,
 
Your hypothesis is basically correct. The Goose iOS app does nothing explicit about pairing, when it connects it only passes the standard connect options, no bonding/encryption calls anywhere. CoreBluetooth handles the LTK exchange transparently the moment the app touches one of the encrypted fd4b… characteristics. So you're right: the band marks those characteristics as requiring an encrypted link (hence your _CBATTError 15_), and on iOS the bond "just happens."

So the sequence that works is: connect > (link gets encrypted/bonded) > discover services > write the client-hello to fd4b0002 > then setNotifyValue on fd4b0003/0004/0005/0007. 
If you subscribe before the hello, you'll get an encrypted-but-mute channel and think the bond failed when it didn't.
